brief: Kubernetes architecture: API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager, kubelet and the reconciliation model

outline.title: Kubernetes architecture fundamentals
outline.summary: You will be able to explain how the API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager and kubelet cooperate to turn a manifest into running containers, and use that model to reason about what happens when a component is slow or down.
outline.prompt: I want to understand how Kubernetes components fit together and how the reconciliation model works so that I can predict cluster behaviour and reason about failures instead of treating the cluster as a black box.

modules.title: Control plane and nodes
modules.objective: Identify each core Kubernetes component, where it runs, and what it is responsible for.
concepts: static pods for control plane components

bank.prompt: Your kubeadm cluster has three control plane nodes and five worker nodes, all with default settings. A developer deploys an ordinary web app with 10 replicas and no tolerations. Where will its pods run?
bank.reference: kubeadm puts a NoSchedule taint on control plane nodes, so pods without a matching toleration land only on workers. The tempting mistake is assuming every node is an equal scheduling target, when taints exclude control plane nodes by default.
options: Only on the five workers, because kubeadm taints control plane nodes so ordinary pods are not scheduled there
Spread across all eight nodes, because the scheduler treats every registered node as equal capacity
On the control plane nodes first, because pods there sit closest to the API server and etcd
On whichever node the developer's kubectl command happened to connect to when applying

bank.prompt: You apply a Deployment with 3 replicas. The Deployment object exists, but kubectl get pods shows no pods at all, not even Pending ones. Which component is most likely not doing its job?
bank.reference: The Deployment and ReplicaSet controllers in kube-controller-manager turn a Deployment into a ReplicaSet and then into Pod objects. If the scheduler were broken, the pods would still exist but sit in Pending with no node assigned.
options: kube-scheduler, which must place pods on nodes before they appear in the API
kube-controller-manager, whose Deployment and ReplicaSet controllers create the Pod objects
The kubelet on each worker, which creates Pod objects once it has spare capacity
kube-proxy, which registers newly created pods with the API server

bank.prompt: A colleague says the scheduler starts the containers on the node it picks for a new pod. Correct this by explaining what the scheduler does and what the kubelet does for that pod.
bank.reference: The scheduler only chooses a suitable node and records that decision (the binding or nodeName) through the API server; it never touches containers. The kubelet on that node watches the API server, sees the pod assigned to it, has the container runtime pull images and start the containers, and reports the pod's status back.

bank.prompt: On a new managed cluster from a cloud provider, kubectl get nodes lists only your worker nodes, and kube-system contains no kube-apiserver or etcd pods. What is the best explanation?
bank.reference: With a managed control plane, the provider operates the API server, etcd, scheduler and controller managers on machines you never see, and you reach them only through the API endpoint. The components still exist and still do their jobs; they are simply not on your nodes.
options: The control plane runs as hidden host processes on your worker nodes, outside any pod
Managed clusters drop etcd and the scheduler because the provider's cloud API replaces them
The provider runs the control plane on its own infrastructure and exposes only the API endpoint
The control plane pods sit in a restricted namespace that your RBAC role is not allowed to list

bank.concept: static pods for control plane components
bank.prompt: On a kubeadm control plane node you run kubectl delete pod for the kube-scheduler pod in kube-system. It reappears within seconds with the same name. Why?
bank.reference: kubeadm runs the scheduler as a static pod defined by a file in the kubelet's manifest directory; the API object is only a mirror, so the kubelet recreates it and the container keeps running. Assuming a Deployment manages it is the common mistake: static pods have no controller behind them in the API.
options: A Deployment in kube-system notices the missing replica and creates a new scheduler pod
The API server refuses to delete system pods and restores the object from etcd
The ReplicaSet controller in kube-controller-manager recreates any deleted kube-system pod
It is a mirror of a static pod that the node's kubelet runs from a local manifest file

bank.prompt: You run a pod that serves traffic behind a ClusterIP Service. Name the components on the worker node that make this work and say what each one contributes.
bank.reference: The kubelet registers the node, runs the pod and reports its status; the container runtime (such as containerd or CRI-O) pulls images and runs the containers for the kubelet; kube-proxy programs network rules so traffic to the Service's ClusterIP reaches the pod. A good answer may also mention the CNI plugin that gives the pod its network.

bank.prompt: The diagram shows a self-managed cluster whose only control plane node has just lost power. What happens to the app pods already running on the three workers during the next ten minutes?
bank.reference: Kubelets and the container runtime keep existing containers running locally, and kube-proxy's already-programmed rules keep routing traffic. What is lost is everything that needs the control plane: kubectl, scheduling and controllers replacing pods. Kubelets do not coordinate among themselves to take over scheduling.
options: They keep running and serving traffic, but no new pods are scheduled and lost pods are not replaced
They stop within seconds, because kubelets need constant instructions from the API server to keep containers alive
They keep running, and the kubelets elect a temporary leader that schedules replacements for failed pods
They keep running, but Service traffic stops because the API server proxies every request to pods

bank.prompt: In the kubeadm cluster shown in the diagram, you deploy a log-agent DaemonSet with no tolerations. Its pods appear on the three workers but not on the two control plane nodes, even though those nodes run a kubelet. Why?
bank.reference: kubeadm taints control plane nodes with NoSchedule, and the DaemonSet's pods lack a matching toleration, so they are kept off those nodes. Control plane nodes are ordinary registered nodes with working kubelets; the taint, not a missing label or a special kubelet mode, is what excludes them.
options: DaemonSets only target nodes carrying a worker role label unless a nodeSelector says otherwise
The control plane nodes carry a NoSchedule taint that the DaemonSet's pods do not tolerate
The scheduler removes control plane nodes from the list of nodes it receives from the API
Control plane kubelets only accept static pods and silently reject pods created through the API

bank.prompt: On a cloud cluster configured with an external cloud provider, you create a Service of type LoadBalancer. Its external IP stays pending, and no load balancer appears in the cloud console. Which component's logs should you check first?
bank.reference: With an external cloud provider, the cloud-controller-manager runs the controllers that talk to the cloud API, including the one that creates load balancers for LoadBalancer Services. kube-proxy only programs node-local rules for traffic and never calls the cloud API.
options: kube-proxy, which creates the cloud load balancer when it programs Service rules
The kubelet on the node hosting the backend pods, which requests the load balancer
cloud-controller-manager, whose service controller provisions cloud load balancers
kube-scheduler, which must place the Service on a node before the IP is assigned

bank.prompt: The diagram shows the components involved when you run kubectl apply for a new Deployment. Describe, in order, which components act until containers are running, and say which of them read or write etcd directly.
bank.reference: kubectl sends the Deployment to the API server, which validates it and stores it in etcd. The controller manager's Deployment and ReplicaSet controllers create a ReplicaSet and Pods via the API server, the scheduler binds each pod to a node, and that node's kubelet has the container runtime start the containers and reports status. Only the API server talks to etcd; every other component works through the API server.

bank.prompt: Your team runs a managed Kubernetes cluster from a cloud provider and needs to change an API server setting, such as enabling audit logging. How do you make the change?
bank.reference: In a managed control plane the provider owns the control plane machines, so API server settings are exposed only through the provider's own configuration, and only for the options it chooses to support. Editing a static pod manifest is the self-managed kubeadm approach and is impossible when you cannot reach those machines.
options: SSH into a control plane node and edit the kube-apiserver static pod manifest
Use the provider's cluster configuration options, since you have no access to the control plane machines
Run kubectl edit on the kube-apiserver Deployment in the kube-system namespace
Create a ConfigMap named kube-apiserver in kube-system, which the API server reloads automatically

bank.prompt: Your team is choosing between a self-managed kubeadm cluster and a cloud provider's managed control plane. Explain what operational work the managed option removes, what control you give up, and what you remain responsible for.
bank.reference: The provider runs and keeps available the API server, etcd, scheduler and controller managers, including their upgrades and etcd backups. You give up direct access to those machines, their flags and parts of their logs, and you are limited to the versions and settings the provider offers. You still own worker nodes (unless the provider also manages them), workloads, RBAC, networking add-ons and upgrade timing.

bank.concept: static pods for control plane components
bank.prompt: On a single control plane kubeadm cluster, you edit the kube-apiserver manifest in the kubelet's manifest directory and mistype a flag. Now every kubectl command fails with connection refused. What is the right way to recover?
bank.reference: The API server is a static pod: the kubelet watches the manifest file and restarts the pod whenever it changes, with no API server needed. Any fix through kubectl is impossible because the API server is the thing that is down, and no Deployment or controller manages it.
options: Run kubectl edit on the kube-apiserver pod in kube-system and correct the flag there
Restart kube-controller-manager so its controllers recreate a healthy API server pod
Correct the manifest file on the node, and the kubelet will restart the API server from it
Wait for the kube-apiserver Deployment to roll back to its previous healthy revision

bank.concept: static pods for control plane components
bank.prompt: kubeadm runs the API server, scheduler, controller manager and etcd as static pods instead of as a Deployment. Explain why this design is needed to bring up a cluster.
bank.reference: A Deployment only works once the API server, etcd, controller manager and scheduler already exist, which is a chicken-and-egg problem. Static pods are run by the kubelet directly from local manifest files with no API server, so the kubelet can start the control plane itself; mirror pods then make them visible in the API once it is up.

bank.prompt: A freshly joined worker shows NotReady. The kubelet is running and reaching the API server, but its log says the container runtime network is not ready because no CNI configuration was found. What is missing?
bank.reference: The kubelet reports the node NotReady while the runtime says pod networking is unavailable, which happens until a CNI plugin is installed and configured. kube-proxy only handles Service rules and is not what gates Ready, and the scheduler places pods, not nodes.
options: The kube-proxy pod for that node, which must start before a node can report Ready
A scheduler decision that assigns the new node to the cluster's pool of Ready nodes
An approval entry in etcd that an administrator must add for every newly joined node
A pod network (CNI) plugin installed and configured for that node

bank.prompt: Pods on one worker cannot reach any Service by its ClusterIP, while connecting directly to a backend pod's IP works. Pods on other workers reach the same Services fine, and the cluster uses kube-proxy. Where should you look first?
bank.reference: kube-proxy runs on each node and programs the local rules, such as iptables or IPVS, that translate ClusterIPs into pod IPs. If only one node fails while direct pod IPs work, that node's kube-proxy is the prime suspect. The kubelet manages pod lifecycles, not Service routing.
options: The kube-proxy pod on the affected worker, since it programs that node's Service rules
The kubelet on the affected worker, since it routes Service traffic for its own pods
The container runtime on the affected worker, since it translates ClusterIPs for containers
The kube-scheduler, since it assigns each Service's traffic to particular nodes

modules.title: The API server and etcd
modules.objective: Explain why every component talks through the API server and how cluster state is stored in etcd.
concepts: api server as single entry point
etcd as the source of truth

bank.concept: api server as single entry point
bank.prompt: A colleague asks why the scheduler records a pod's node assignment by calling the API server instead of writing it into etcd itself, since etcd is where the data ends up anyway. What is the main reason?
bank.reference: All components, including the scheduler, read and write cluster state only through the API server, which is the single client of etcd and applies authentication, authorization, admission and validation to every request. Direct etcd writes are not merely discouraged: they would skip all of those checks and the API's versioning and defaulting.
options: The API server is the only component that talks to etcd, so every write passes authentication, authorization, admission and validation
Going through the API server is only a convention; direct etcd writes behave the same way but are harder to audit
etcd accepts connections only from processes on its own control plane node, and the scheduler may run on another node
The scheduler is read-only by design and must ask the controller manager to perform any writes on its behalf

bank.prompt: The diagram shows the stages a create request passes through inside the API server. A user's pod creation is rejected by a validating admission webhook because a required label is missing. Which statement about that request is true?
bank.reference: Requests are authenticated, then authorized, then go through mutating admission, schema validation and validating admission, and only then are persisted to etcd. A rejection at validating admission means the earlier stages passed and the object was never stored, so there is nothing to roll back.
options: Authentication and authorization succeeded, mutating admission already ran, and nothing was written to etcd
The pod was written to etcd first and then rolled back once the validating webhook objected
Authorization was skipped, because an admission webhook replaces the RBAC check for that resource
Mutating admission had not run yet, because validation always happens before any mutation

bank.concept: etcd as the source of truth
bank.prompt: During an upgrade, every API server instance in your cluster is down for five minutes. When they come back, all Deployments, Services and Secrets are still there. Explain why nothing was lost, and what kind of failure would actually lose this state.
bank.reference: The API server is stateless; all cluster objects are persisted in etcd, so restarting or losing API servers loses nothing and they simply serve etcd's contents again. State is actually lost only if etcd's data is lost, for example losing a majority of members' disks or corrupting the data without a usable backup or snapshot.

bank.prompt: In the timeline, controllers A and B both read the same Deployment at resourceVersion 100, change different fields locally, and each sends a full update carrying the resourceVersion it read. A's update is stored first. What happens to B's update?
bank.reference: Updates use optimistic concurrency: the write succeeds only if the object's current resourceVersion still matches the one sent. After A's write the object is at a newer version, so B gets a 409 Conflict and must re-read and retry; the API server does not silently overwrite or merge full updates.
options: It is rejected with a conflict, and B must read the latest version and reapply its change
It is stored and silently overwrites A's change, because the last writer always wins
The API server merges both changes, because they touch different fields of the object
It waits in a queue until A's change has finished reconciling, and is then applied

bank.prompt: Controllers need to react within moments when, for example, a pod they manage is deleted. How do they typically learn about such changes?
bank.reference: Controllers list once and then hold a watch on the API server, receiving added, modified and deleted events as they happen, starting after a known resourceVersion. They do not talk to etcd directly, and frequent full lists would be slow and expensive compared to streaming only the changes.
options: They open a watch on the API server, which streams change events after the resourceVersion they last saw
They open a watch directly on etcd, since watching through the API server would add too much latency
They list all relevant objects every second and diff each result against their previous list
The API server calls each controller's webhook endpoint whenever a relevant object is written

bank.concept: api server as single entry point
bank.prompt: The diagram shows a proposal to let kubelets read their pod specs straight from etcd to take load off the API server. Explain two important things the cluster would lose if this were done.
bank.reference: Any two of: every node would need etcd credentials that expose the whole cluster state including all Secrets, so one compromised node exposes everything; the API server's per-node authorization, which limits a kubelet to objects for its own node, would be bypassed; kubelets would depend on etcd's internal storage format instead of the versioned, defaulted API; and the API server's watch cache would no longer absorb reads, likely increasing load on etcd rather than reducing it.

bank.prompt: A controller's watch connection drops and it reconnects an hour later, asking to resume from the resourceVersion it last saw. The API server answers 410 Gone because that history has been compacted. What should the controller do?
bank.reference: 410 Gone means the requested point in history is no longer available, so the client must relist to rebuild its view of current state and then watch from the list's resourceVersion; client informers do this automatically. Retrying the old version will never succeed, and there is no full event replay, because etcd compacts old revisions.
options: List the objects again to get current state and a fresh resourceVersion, then start a new watch from there
Keep retrying the watch with the same resourceVersion until the API server is able to serve it again
Resume watching from resourceVersion 0, which replays every event since the cluster was created
Ignore the gap, because the missed events are replayed automatically on the next resync from etcd

bank.concept: api server as single entry point
bank.prompt: The Deployment controller creates ReplicaSets, the ReplicaSet controller creates pods, and the scheduler assigns those pods to nodes, yet none of these components ever call each other. How do they coordinate?
bank.reference: Components are decoupled: they communicate only by reading, watching and writing API objects, so a ReplicaSet written by one controller is an event for another, and a pod without a node is work for the scheduler. There is no direct component-to-component call chain or shared message bus; the API server is the hub.
options: Each one writes and watches objects through the API server, so one component's output becomes another's input
The controller manager runs an internal message bus that the scheduler and the kubelets subscribe to
Each component calls the next one's API directly, and the API server only records the final outcome
They share an in-memory cache on the leader control plane node that every component reads from

bank.prompt: After cluster credentials are rotated, one engineer gets 401 Unauthorized from every kubectl command, while another gets 403 Forbidden only when deleting pods. Diagnose each case, and say which one granting an RBAC role could fix.
bank.reference: 401 means authentication failed: the API server could not establish who the first engineer is, likely because their certificate or token is expired or no longer trusted, so they need new credentials. 403 means the second engineer was authenticated but authorization denied the delete, so only the 403 case can be fixed by granting an RBAC role; RBAC is never consulted when authentication fails.

bank.prompt: A mutating webhook injects a logging sidecar into every pod. A validating admission policy rejects pods with any container lacking a memory limit. The injected sidecar has no limit, but the user's own container does. What happens when the user creates a pod?
bank.reference: Validating admission runs after all mutating admission, on the final object that would be stored, so it sees the sidecar without a limit and rejects the whole request before anything reaches etcd. The tempting mistake is thinking validation only checks what the user sent; it checks the mutated result.
options: The pod is rejected, because validating admission runs after mutation and sees the injected sidecar
The pod is accepted, because validation checks only the spec the user originally submitted
The pod is accepted without the sidecar, since mutations that fail validation are quietly reverted
The pod is stored, then deleted moments later once the validating policy notices the sidecar

bank.concept: etcd as the source of truth
bank.prompt: After a disk failure, an operator restores etcd from a snapshot taken two hours ago and restarts the API servers. A ConfigMap was created one hour ago, and nothing has re-created it since. What does a get for that ConfigMap return now?
bank.reference: etcd is the single source of truth, so restoring an older snapshot rolls cluster state back to that point and objects created afterwards no longer exist. The API server keeps no durable copy of its own, and kubelets do not push objects back into the API, which is why recent etcd backups matter.
options: Not found, because the API server serves only what etcd currently contains
It still appears, because the API server re-populates etcd from its memory
It still appears, because kubelets that mounted it report it back to the API
It appears with an error status until the API server reconciles the snapshot gap

bank.concept: etcd as the source of truth
bank.prompt: Your platform team wants to grow etcd from 3 members to 4 to make cluster state safer. Writes need a majority of members, \( q = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor + 1 \). Explain whether adding a fourth member helps, and what you would recommend instead.
bank.reference: Four members need a quorum of three, so the cluster still tolerates only one member failure, the same as three members, while adding replication work and one more machine that can fail. Recommend staying at three or moving to five, which tolerates two failures, and above all keeping regular, tested etcd backups.

bank.prompt: A controller updates only the status of a Deployment; nobody has touched its spec. Comparing the object's metadata before and after this write, what do you expect to see?
bank.reference: resourceVersion changes on every write to the object, including status updates, because it tracks the stored version used for concurrency and watches. generation tracks changes to the desired state in the spec, so a status-only update leaves it alone; confusing the two leads to wrong assumptions about when the spec changed.
options: resourceVersion changes, while generation stays the same
Both resourceVersion and generation increase by one
generation increases, while resourceVersion stays the same
Neither changes, because status writes are not versioned

bank.prompt: Your operator's logs fill with errors saying the object has been modified and you should apply your changes to the latest version, and some of its updates never take effect. Explain what is causing this and the right way to handle it.
bank.reference: These are optimistic concurrency conflicts: the operator sends updates based on a stale resourceVersion because something else wrote the object after it was read. The fix is to re-read the latest object, reapply the change and retry (or requeue), and to check whether two controllers are fighting over the same fields; forcing writes by dropping the resourceVersion would silently clobber other writers.

bank.prompt: Imagine each of 500 kubelets listing its pods every 2 seconds instead of watching: \( 500 / 2 = 250 \) list requests per second, almost all returning unchanged data. What is the main thing switching to watches changes?
bank.reference: A watch replaces repeated full lists with a single long-lived connection over which the API server sends only added, modified or deleted events, so cost scales with the rate of change rather than with polling frequency times object count. It does not route traffic around the API server or make multi-object changes atomic.
options: Each kubelet holds one long-lived stream that carries only changes, so quiet periods cost almost nothing
The lists move from the API server to etcd directly, so the API server no longer carries this load
Kubelets still list every 2 seconds, but responses are compressed so they use less bandwidth
Changes become transactional across objects, so kubelets see related updates as a single event

bank.prompt: The diagram shows 200 clients watching pods through one API server instance running with default settings. Roughly how does that instance get pod changes from etcd to deliver to all of them?
bank.reference: By default the API server maintains a watch cache fed by roughly one etcd watch per resource type, and serves many client watches from that cache, which shields etcd from scaling with the number of watchers. Assuming one etcd watch per client is the common mistake; clients never connect to etcd at all.
options: It keeps a small number of watches on etcd and fans events out to all clients from its watch cache
It opens a separate etcd watch for every client, so etcd tracks around 200 pod watches
It polls etcd for pod changes every second and pushes the differences out to its clients
It gives each client the etcd endpoint so events stream from etcd without passing through it

modules.title: Desired state and reconciliation
modules.objective: Describe how declarative objects with spec and status drive controllers that continuously converge actual state toward desired state.
concepts: built-in controllers in the controller manager

bank.prompt: kubectl get deployment web -o yaml shows spec.replicas: 3 and status.readyReplicas: 2. Which reading of these two fields is correct?
bank.reference: Spec is the desired state written by users or tools; status is the observed state reported by controllers. A gap between them means reconciliation is in progress or blocked, not that spec is a ceiling or that the roles are reversed.
options: You asked for three replicas and controllers observe two ready, so the system is still converging or something is blocking it.
Two replicas were requested, and spec.replicas is the maximum the Deployment may scale up to under heavy load.
Status is stale because kubectl caches it on the client, so the real number of ready pods is already three.
Status was written by you at creation time, and spec is updated by controllers to show what the cluster has.

bank.prompt: During an incident you run kubectl scale deployment api --replicas=10. The manifest in git says replicas: 3, and CI runs client-side kubectl apply -f with that manifest on every merge. An hour later a teammate merges an unrelated change. What happens to the replica count?
bank.reference: The manifest declares replicas: 3, and apply sets declared fields that differ from the live object, so the imperative scale is overwritten. The common misconception is that apply only diffs old file against new file; it also compares against the live object for fields the file declares.
options: It returns to 3, because apply re-asserts the declared value and the imperative scale was never recorded in git.
It stays at 10, because apply only changes fields that differ between the previous and new versions of the file.
It stays at 10, because the live value is newer than the file and Kubernetes keeps the most recent write by timestamp.
The apply fails with an error, because the live replica count no longer matches the last applied configuration.

bank.prompt: The diagram shows a ReplicaSet controller's reconcile loop. The controller was down for five minutes, during which three of its pods were deleted and its spec was edited twice. When it restarts, what does it do?
bank.reference: Controllers are level-triggered: they act on the difference between current desired and observed state, not on a history of events, so missed events do not matter. The tempting mistake is to think of controllers as event replayers that need every intermediate change.
options: Lists current objects, compares the latest spec with the pods that exist now, and creates or deletes pods to close any gap.
Replays the queued deletion and edit events in order, applying each one as if it had been seen live.
Waits for a new deletion event before acting, because the earlier events were missed while it was down.
Restores the deleted pods from an etcd snapshot taken before it stopped, then resumes processing events.

bank.concept: built-in controllers in the controller manager
bank.prompt: You run kubectl delete pod on one pod owned by a ReplicaSet with replicas: 3. Within seconds a new pod with a different name appears. Explain which component created it and why, in terms of desired and observed state.
bank.reference: The ReplicaSet controller, running in kube-controller-manager, observes only two matching pods while the spec still desires three, so it creates a new Pod object through the API server (with a new generated name); the scheduler then assigns it and the kubelet runs it. Deleting a pod changes actual state, not desired state.

bank.prompt: kubectl apply printed deployment.apps/web configured, yet kubectl get pods shows old-image pods for another minute. A teammate concludes the apply partly failed. What is the best explanation?
bank.reference: A successful apply means the desired state was validated and persisted; actually rolling pods happens afterwards through independent asynchronous controllers. The misconception is treating apply as a synchronous command that completes the change before returning.
options: Apply only records the new desired state; controllers, the scheduler and kubelets converge on it asynchronously afterwards.
The API server writes changes in batches, so the object in etcd is not updated until the next batch is flushed.
kubectl get pods reads from a client-side cache that only refreshes from the API server every few minutes.
The apply partly failed, and the API server will keep retrying the write to etcd in the background until it succeeds.

bank.concept: built-in controllers in the controller manager
bank.prompt: You change the container image in a Deployment's pod template. Which description of how the built-in controllers carry out this change is accurate?
bank.reference: Controllers are layered: the Deployment controller manages ReplicaSets (one per template), and ReplicaSet controllers manage pods. Pods are not mutated in place for a template change, and the kubelet and scheduler only act on individual Pod objects.
options: The Deployment controller creates a new ReplicaSet and shifts replica counts toward it; the ReplicaSet controller creates and deletes pods.
The Deployment controller patches the image on each running pod in place, one at a time, honouring maxUnavailable.
The kubelet on each node notices the template change and restarts its containers in place with the new image.
The scheduler detects the template change, deletes old pods and places new ones on the least loaded nodes.

bank.prompt: During a slow rollout, an impatient colleague edits the Deployment and changes status.readyReplicas from 1 to 3, hoping traffic will be served sooner. Predict what happens and explain what they should change instead.
bank.reference: Nothing about the pods changes: status is a report of observed state written by controllers, so the edit is ignored or quickly overwritten with the real observed value (Deployment status is a separate subresource). To influence behaviour they must change spec, such as replicas, template or strategy, or fix why pods are not becoming ready.

bank.prompt: A deploy script edits a Deployment's spec, immediately reads status, sees updatedReplicas equal to replicas, and declares success. Later the old version is still running. Which check would have prevented this false success?
bank.reference: generation increments when spec changes, and the controller sets observedGeneration when it has processed that spec; until they match, status still describes the previous spec. A rising generation only shows the API server stored the change, not that any controller acted on it.
options: Wait until status.observedGeneration reaches metadata.generation before trusting the other status fields.
Wait until metadata.resourceVersion stops changing between two consecutive reads of the object.
Compare spec.replicas with status.replicas, since any mismatch means the new spec was rejected.
Check that metadata.generation has increased, which proves the controller has applied the new spec.

bank.prompt: Running kubectl create -f app.yaml twice fails the second time with AlreadyExists, while running kubectl apply -f app.yaml twice succeeds and changes nothing the second time. Why does this difference matter for automated pipelines?
bank.reference: Declarative apply is idempotent: it describes what should exist and only changes differences, so pipelines can rerun it freely. Both commands go through the API server, and apply patches rather than deleting and recreating objects.
options: Apply declares the end state, so rerunning it is safe and converges; create is a one-shot action tied to current state.
Apply skips validation on later runs, so pipelines finish faster when the objects already exist in the cluster.
Create writes straight to etcd while apply goes through the API server, so only apply changes are audited.
Apply deletes and recreates the object on each run, guaranteeing the live object exactly matches the file.

bank.prompt: Your runbook says to restart an app by deleting its pods one by one with kubectl delete pod. A colleague proposes kubectl rollout restart, which updates an annotation in the Deployment's pod template. Compare the two approaches as imperative versus declarative changes.
bank.reference: Deleting pods is an imperative action on instances: desired state is unchanged, the ReplicaSet just replaces them, nothing is recorded, and no rollout safeguards apply, so deleting too fast can cause an outage. Rollout restart changes the desired state (the template), so the Deployment controller performs a controlled rolling update that respects the strategy and is recorded in rollout history.

bank.prompt: A ReplicaSet has replicas: 3, selector app=web, and three healthy pods. Someone manually creates a standalone pod labelled app=web with no owner reference. What happens?
bank.reference: The ReplicaSet reconciles on the current count of matching pods, acquiring unowned pods that match its selector and then deleting extras to reach the desired count. It does not track its own creations by name, and it never rewrites its spec to fit reality.
options: The controller counts four matching pods against three desired, adopts the new pod and deletes one to return to three.
Nothing, because the controller only manages pods it created itself and tracks them by name in its own records.
The pod is rejected at admission, because the selector already has its full count of replicas running.
The controller raises its spec to four replicas, because spec must always match every pod the selector finds.

bank.prompt: Your custom controller's reconcile function creates a ConfigMap with a generated name every time it runs. After a day, each custom resource owns dozens of ConfigMaps, although users edited each resource only once. Diagnose the design flaw in terms of how reconcile loops are triggered.
bank.reference: Reconcile is level-triggered and runs many times per object, on periodic resyncs, controller restarts, error retries, status updates and coalesced events, not once per user edit. It must be idempotent: check whether the ConfigMap already exists (for example via a deterministic name or owner reference) and create or update only when the observed state differs.

bank.concept: built-in controllers in the controller manager
bank.prompt: The diagram shows the ownership chain for Deployment web. You run kubectl delete replicaset web-6f8c with default options. What happens next?
bank.reference: Default deletion cascades, so the garbage collector removes the pods owned by the ReplicaSet, while the Deployment controller sees no ReplicaSet for its template and creates one, which then creates pods. Deployments never own pods directly; they always work through ReplicaSets.
options: The three pods are garbage collected, and the Deployment controller creates a new ReplicaSet that creates three pods.
The three pods keep running as orphans, and the Deployment adopts them directly since no ReplicaSet remains.
The Deployment is marked failed and stays without pods until someone reapplies its manifest to the cluster.
The API server refuses the delete, because a ReplicaSet owned by a Deployment cannot be removed directly.

bank.concept: built-in controllers in the controller manager
bank.prompt: kube-controller-manager is down for ten minutes while the API server, scheduler and kubelets stay healthy. Meanwhile someone scales Deployment A from 3 to 6 and someone deletes a pod of Deployment B. Predict what happens during the outage and after recovery.
bank.reference: During the outage existing pods keep running and kubelets still restart crashed containers, and the API server accepts the scale, but no new pods appear for A and B's deleted pod is not replaced, because the Deployment and ReplicaSet controllers live in the controller manager. After recovery the controllers observe the gaps between spec and actual state and create the missing pods without anyone reapplying anything.

modules.title: Scheduler and kubelet
modules.objective: Trace how the scheduler binds a pod to a node and how the kubelet makes it run through the container runtime.
concepts: node status and heartbeats via leases

bank.prompt: A pod requests 4 CPU. One node has only 2 CPU of allocatable capacity left, but it already has the image cached and the lowest overall load. How does the scheduler treat that node for this pod?
bank.reference: Filtering is a hard feasibility check: a node whose free allocatable resources cannot fit the pod's requests is excluded before scoring, so a cached image or low load cannot rescue it. The tempting mistake is treating resource fit as a soft preference that only lowers a node's score.
options: It is removed during filtering, so it is never scored or chosen
It gets a low score but can still win if other nodes score lower
It can be chosen, and the kubelet then evicts pods to make room
It is held back until the next cycle, then retried with fresh scores

bank.prompt: The diagram shows filter results and per-plugin scores for three nodes. The final score is a weighted sum \( \text{score}(n) = \sum_i w_i \, s_i(n) \), with the weights shown. Which node does the scheduler pick?
bank.reference: Only node-2 and node-3 pass filtering. Weighted totals are 90 + 2 x 40 = 170 for node-2 and 40 + 2 x 80 = 200 for node-3, so node-3 wins. Adding raw scores without weights (130 vs 120) wrongly favours node-2.
options: node-3, because it has the highest weighted total among nodes that passed filtering
node-2, because it has the highest unweighted total among nodes that passed filtering
node-1, because a node that fails one filter is still scored on the others
No node yet, because a tie between the two feasible nodes is broken on the next cycle

bank.prompt: The scheduler process crashes right after deciding a pending pod should go to node-7, but before it has written the binding to the API server. Predict what happens to the pod and whether node-7 starts it.
bank.reference: Nothing was recorded, so the pod's spec.nodeName is still empty and it stays Pending; node-7's kubelet never sees it because kubelets only act on pods bound to them. When the scheduler restarts or another replica takes leadership, it schedules the pod again from scratch and may choose a different node.

bank.prompt: The scheduler has just bound a pod to node-4. How does the kubelet on node-4 find out that it should start this pod?
bank.reference: Each kubelet keeps a watch on the API server filtered to pods assigned to its node, so the binding itself is the signal. The common misconception is that the scheduler talks to the kubelet directly; in fact components coordinate only through objects in the API server, and nothing but the API server talks to etcd.
options: It watches the API server for pods whose spec.nodeName matches its own node
The scheduler opens a direct connection to the kubelet and sends the pod spec
It reads pod records straight from etcd on a fixed polling interval
The controller manager pushes the pod to the node after the binding

bank.prompt: A newly bound pod shows ImagePullBackOff. Which component actually tried to pull the image and create the containers on the node?
bank.reference: The kubelet decides what should run and asks the container runtime over the Container Runtime Interface to pull images and create sandboxes and containers; the runtime does the pulling. A frequent mistake is thinking the kubelet pulls images itself, which hides where to look for registry or credential errors.
options: The container runtime, such as containerd, acting on kubelet requests over CRI
The kubelet itself, which downloads image layers and forks container processes
The scheduler, which pre-pulls the image onto the node before binding it
The API server, which streams the image from the registry to the node

bank.concept: node status and heartbeats via leases
bank.prompt: Every kubelet frequently renews a Lease object in the kube-node-lease namespace, while it updates the full Node status much less often when nothing changes. Why is the heartbeat split this way?
bank.reference: Writing the large Node status object frequently across many nodes is expensive, so the kubelet renews a tiny Lease as its heartbeat and sends full status only on changes or at a slower interval. The tempting wrong idea is that leases replace node status entirely; both still exist and serve different purposes.
options: A small Lease update is a cheap liveness signal, keeping API server and etcd load low
The Lease grants the kubelet exclusive permission to run containers on its node
The Lease stores the pod list so the scheduler can skip reading Node objects
Node status updates are disabled once leases are on, so the Lease replaces them

bank.concept: node status and heartbeats via leases
bank.prompt: The timeline in the diagram shows a kubelet renewing its node Lease until the node loses network connectivity. Predict what the control plane does once the marked grace period has elapsed, and what that means for the pods on that node.
bank.reference: The node lifecycle controller sees no Lease renewal within the grace period, sets the node's Ready condition to Unknown and adds an unreachable NoExecute taint. Pods without a longer toleration are evicted after their toleration time (about five minutes by default), and their owning controllers create replacements on other nodes, even though the original containers may still be running on the cut-off node.

bank.prompt: A pod is Pending with the event: 0/5 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient memory, 2 node(s) had untolerated taint. A teammate suggests raising the weight of a scoring plugin that favours nodes with free memory. What is the right assessment?
bank.reference: The event means no node passed filtering, so there is nothing to score; the fix must make at least one node feasible, for example lowering the request, adding capacity or tolerating the taint. The tempting error is believing scoring can override a filter failure, or blaming the kubelet when the pod was never bound.
options: It cannot help, because every node failed filtering and scoring only ranks feasible nodes
It will help, because the pod goes to the highest scoring node once weights change
It will help after a few retries, because filter failures turn into low scores over time
It cannot help, because the kubelets on those nodes are rejecting the pod at startup

bank.prompt: Your cluster autoscaler rarely removes nodes because the scheduler spreads pods thinly across all of them, leaving none empty. Explain whether filtering or scoring causes this, and what kind of change would let nodes drain naturally.
bank.reference: This is a scoring effect: all the nodes are feasible, and the default resource scoring prefers less allocated nodes, which spreads load. Switching the resource scoring strategy to prefer more allocated nodes (bin packing, such as the MostAllocated strategy) concentrates pods so some nodes empty out and can be scaled down; changing filters would not alter the preference among feasible nodes.

bank.prompt: Node-3 is cordoned for maintenance. Someone creates a pod manifest that sets spec.nodeName: node-3 directly. What happens?
bank.reference: Cordoning marks the node unschedulable, which is something the scheduler respects; a pod that arrives with nodeName already set is never seen by the scheduler, and node-3's kubelet simply starts it, subject only to its own admission checks such as resource fit. The common belief that a cordon blocks every new pod on the node is wrong.
options: The pod runs on node-3, because setting nodeName bypasses the scheduler that honours cordons
The pod stays Pending until node-3 is uncordoned, then starts there automatically
The scheduler notices the cordon and rebinds the pod to another schedulable node
The API server rejects the pod because cordoned nodes refuse all new bindings

bank.prompt: A pod was bound to a busy node an hour ago. A large, nearly empty node has since joined the cluster. What does the default scheduler do about the existing pod?
bank.reference: The scheduler only acts on pods with no nodeName; once bound, the field is immutable, so moving a pod means deleting it and letting its controller create a replacement, which is what tools like the descheduler do. The tempting misconception is that the scheduler continuously rebalances running pods.
options: Nothing, because binding is a one-time decision and nodeName cannot be changed
It rebinds the pod to the new node on its next scheduling cycle to balance load
It moves the pod live to the new node without restarting its containers
It re-scores all bound pods whenever a node joins and migrates the poorest fits

bank.prompt: A worker node loses connectivity to the API server for ten minutes but the node itself stays healthy. During that time a container in one of its pods crashes; the pod has restartPolicy Always. What does the kubelet do?
bank.reference: The kubelet keeps reconciling the pods it already knows about, so it restarts the crashed container per the restart policy even without the API server; it just cannot receive new assignments or report status. A common mistake is assuming that losing the control plane makes the kubelet kill or freeze workloads.
options: Restarts the container locally, using the pod specs it already has cached
Leaves the container dead, because restarts need approval from the API server
Stops every pod on the node once its Lease can no longer be renewed
Asks the container runtime to pause all containers until the connection returns

bank.prompt: On a kubeadm cluster, the API server runs as a pod on the control plane node, yet the kubelet learns about pods by watching the API server. Explain how the kubelet can start the API server in the first place.
bank.reference: The control plane components run as static pods: the kubelet reads their manifests from a local directory on the node and runs them without needing the API server. Once the API server is up, the kubelet creates read-only mirror pod objects so they appear in the API, but the local files remain the source of truth.

bank.prompt: Your team is moving its nodes from Docker Engine (formerly reached through the dockershim, which was removed in Kubernetes 1.24) to containerd. Developers worry about their images built with docker build. What is the accurate expectation?
bank.reference: Images built with Docker are OCI-compliant, and containerd pulls and runs them unchanged; the removal only affected how the kubelet talks to the runtime, now always through CRI. The frequent fear is that removing dockershim breaks Docker-built images, which conflates the build tool with the node runtime.
options: Existing images keep working, because they are standard OCI images containerd can run
All images must be rebuilt with a containerd-specific tool before the upgrade
Images run only if Docker Engine stays installed on every node as a fallback
Images work, but pods must declare a runtime annotation to use containerd

bank.prompt: The diagram shows the runtime stack on a node with two runtime handlers configured. You want only untrusted tenant pods to run inside lightweight VMs, while all other pods keep using the default handler. What is the usual approach?
bank.reference: RuntimeClass maps a pod to a handler configured in the CRI runtime, so the kubelet and the CRI connection stay the same and only the low-level runtime differs per pod. Swapping the runtime for the whole node isolates everything and loses the per-pod choice, and nodeName only picks a node, not a handler.
options: Define a RuntimeClass for the VM handler and set runtimeClassName on the tenant pods
Run a second kubelet on the node that speaks a different protocol to the VM runtime
Replace containerd with the VM runtime for the whole node so every pod is isolated
Pin the tenant pods with nodeName so the scheduler picks the VM handler for them

bank.concept: node status and heartbeats via leases
bank.prompt: kubectl shows a worker node as NotReady with status Unknown, but when you SSH in, its application containers are still running and serving traffic. Diagnose the most likely cause and explain why the containers kept running.
bank.reference: The kubelet has stopped renewing its Lease and posting status, for example because the kubelet crashed or cannot reach the API server (network issue or expired credentials), so the node controller marked it Unknown after the grace period. The containers keep running because the container runtime manages them independently of the kubelet's connection to the control plane.

modules.title: Following an object end to end
modules.objective: Walk through every component involved when you apply a Deployment, from kubectl to running containers and back to status.
concepts: deployment to replicaset to pod chain
reading the chain with kubectl get and events

bank.prompt: You run kubectl apply -f web.yaml for a brand new Deployment, and within a second it prints that deployment.apps/web was created. What is true at the moment that command returns?
bank.reference: The apply request finishes once the API server has authenticated, authorized, run admission, validated and persisted the object. Controllers then react to it asynchronously. A common misconception is that the ReplicaSet is created in the same request, but the Deployment controller only acts after it sees the stored object through its watch.
options: The API server has admitted, validated and stored the Deployment in etcd; its ReplicaSet and Pods may not exist yet
The Deployment controller has created the ReplicaSet within the same request, but no Pods have been scheduled yet
The scheduler has assigned the Pods to nodes, and the kubelets are now pulling the container images
kubectl has sent the manifest to each node's kubelet, which will now start the containers asynchronously

bank.concept: deployment to replicaset to pod chain
bank.prompt: The diagram shows the components involved after you apply a Deployment. Which component creates the Pod objects that eventually run your containers?
bank.reference: The Deployment controller creates and scales ReplicaSets. The ReplicaSet controller creates the Pod objects. The scheduler only binds existing Pods to nodes, and the kubelet only runs Pods already bound to its node. The tempting mistake is to assume the Deployment controller creates Pods itself, skipping the ReplicaSet layer.
options: The ReplicaSet controller, which watches ReplicaSets and creates Pods through the API server
The Deployment controller, which creates Pods directly from the Deployment's pod template
The scheduler, which creates one Pod per replica on the node it has chosen for it
The kubelet, which creates Pod objects on its node when it sees a new Deployment

bank.prompt: You run kubectl delete deployment web with no extra flags. A few seconds later, its ReplicaSet and its three Pods are also gone. Which mechanism removed them?
bank.reference: Deletion cascades through ownerReferences. With the default background propagation, the Deployment is removed first, then the garbage collector deletes the dependent ReplicaSet, and after that its Pods. The tempting mistake is to think labels drive the cleanup, but it is ownership metadata, not selector matching, that links the objects.
options: The garbage collector saw that their ownerReferences pointed to an owner that no longer exists and deleted them
The Deployment controller deleted the ReplicaSet and Pods by label selector before letting the Deployment go
The API server deleted every object matching the Deployment's selector in the same etcd transaction
The ReplicaSet controller noticed its Deployment was missing, so it scaled to zero and deleted itself

bank.prompt: After you apply a new image tag, kubectl get deployment web -o yaml shows metadata.generation at 7 but status.observedGeneration at 6, and the status counts have not changed for several minutes. What does this tell you, and which component would you suspect first?
bank.reference: The API server stored the new spec, which is why the generation went up. The Deployment controller has not yet processed that spec, because observedGeneration is written by the controller when it reconciles. Suspect the Deployment controller in kube-controller-manager: it may not be running, may have no leader, or may be unable to reach the API server. Nothing further down the chain will change until it reconciles.

bank.concept: reading the chain with kubectl get and events
bank.prompt: A Deployment shows READY 0/3. kubectl get pods shows no Pods for it at all, and kubectl get rs shows its ReplicaSet with DESIRED 3 and CURRENT 0. What is the most useful next step?
bank.reference: The ReplicaSet exists but no Pods were created, so the failure is at Pod creation, and the ReplicaSet controller records it as events on the ReplicaSet. Typical causes are a ResourceQuota or an admission policy rejecting the Pod. Scheduling problems are the tempting answer, but they would show up as Pods stuck in Pending, and here no Pods exist to schedule.
options: Describe the ReplicaSet and read its events, looking for FailedCreate messages from quota or admission rejections
Describe the Deployment's Pods and read their events, looking for FailedScheduling messages from the scheduler
Check the kubelet logs on the worker nodes for image pull or container runtime errors during startup
Check the scheduler logs to find out why it could not place the three Pods onto any available node

bank.concept: deployment to replicaset to pod chain
bank.prompt: You change only the container image in a Deployment and apply it. Afterwards kubectl get rs shows two ReplicaSets for that Deployment, one of them with 0 replicas. Explain what the Deployment controller did, and why the old ReplicaSet is still there.
bank.reference: The changed pod template has a new template hash, so the Deployment controller created a new ReplicaSet. During the rolling update it scaled the new one up and the old one down, keeping within its surge and unavailability limits. The old ReplicaSet is kept at zero replicas as revision history, so a rollback can scale it back up. How many old ReplicaSets are kept is limited by the revision history limit.

bank.prompt: A new Pod moves from Pending to Running, and its Ready condition becomes true. Which component writes the container states and the readiness condition into the Pod's status?
bank.reference: The kubelet runs the containers through the container runtime, runs the probes, and patches the Pod's status through the API server. The container runtime only talks to the kubelet over CRI and never to the API server. That is the misconception behind the most tempting wrong answer.
options: The kubelet on the Pod's node, which reports what it observes through the API server
The scheduler, which updates the Pod's status when it binds the Pod to a node
The ReplicaSet controller, which marks its Pods ready as it counts its replicas
The container runtime, which writes container state directly to the API server

bank.prompt: You apply an updated Deployment manifest, and kubectl prints an error saying an admission webhook denied the request. What state is the Deployment in now?
bank.reference: Admission runs before the API server persists the object, so a rejected request never reaches etcd and no watch event is sent. The live object stays exactly as it was. A tempting mistake is to think the object is stored with some failed marker, but Kubernetes has no stored but rejected state for a write.
options: The change was never persisted, so the live Deployment is unchanged and no controller saw the update
The new spec was stored but flagged as rejected, so the Deployment controller skips it until it is fixed
The new spec was stored, and the rollout will start, but each new Pod will be rejected when it is created
The change was written to etcd and then rolled back, so watchers briefly saw the new spec before it reverted

bank.prompt: During an incident, someone ran kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=5. The manifest in git still says replicas: 3. Your pipeline later runs kubectl apply on that unchanged manifest. Predict the replica count afterwards and explain why.
bank.reference: The count goes back to 3. apply sends the fields your manifest declares. Because replicas is declared and the live value differs, the patch overwrites it. The Deployment controller then scales the ReplicaSet down. To let kubectl scale or an autoscaler own the replica count, leave replicas out of the applied manifest.

bank.concept: deployment to replicaset to pod chain
bank.prompt: The diagram shows a Deployment with 4 replicas partway through a rolling update. Its new Pods crash on startup. Assuming the default rolling update rounding, what will the Deployment controller do next?
bank.reference: 25 percent of 4 gives a surge of 1 and an unavailability of 1. That allows at most 5 Pods in total and requires at least 3 available. With 5 Pods and only 3 available, the controller can neither add Pods nor remove old ones, so the rollout stalls. After the progress deadline, the Progressing condition turns false. Kubernetes does not roll back automatically, which is the tempting misconception.
options: Hold both ReplicaSets where they are, and eventually report that the rollout exceeded its progress deadline
Automatically roll back by scaling the new ReplicaSet to zero and the old ReplicaSet back up to four
Keep scaling down the old ReplicaSet so the rollout can finish, even though the new Pods are not ready
Delete the failing new ReplicaSet and create a fresh one to retry the rollout with new Pods

bank.concept: deployment to replicaset to pod chain
bank.prompt: Under load, a teammate runs kubectl scale on the ReplicaSet web-7d9f8c6b5, setting it to 10 replicas. That ReplicaSet is owned by Deployment web, which specifies 3 replicas. What happens over the next few seconds?
bank.reference: The Deployment is the desired state for its ReplicaSets. Its controller keeps reconciling the ReplicaSet's replica count back to the Deployment's value, so the scale-up is undone almost immediately. The tempting mistake is to think the change sticks until the next apply, but reconciliation is continuous and does not wait for user actions.
options: The Deployment controller sees the mismatch and scales the ReplicaSet back to 3, so the extra Pods are removed
The ReplicaSet stays at 10 until the Deployment manifest is applied again and resets the count to 3
The Deployment controller updates the Deployment's own replicas field to 10 to match its ReplicaSet
The ReplicaSet detaches from the Deployment and from now on is managed independently at 10 replicas

bank.prompt: You run kubectl delete deployment web --cascade=orphan. The Deployment is removed, but its ReplicaSet and its 3 Pods keep running. You then apply the original Deployment manifest again, unchanged. What happens?
bank.reference: Orphaning removes the ownerReferences, leaving the ReplicaSet ownerless. Controllers adopt ownerless objects that match their selector, so the new Deployment takes over the ReplicaSet. Because its template hash matches, it becomes the current ReplicaSet, and its Pods are kept. The tempting mistake is to think ownership is fixed to the old UID, when in fact adoption re-links the objects by setting a new ownerReference.
options: The new Deployment adopts the existing ReplicaSet because it matches the selector and template, so no new Pods are created
The new Deployment creates a second ReplicaSet with 3 more Pods, because the old one belonged to a different UID
The garbage collector deletes the orphaned ReplicaSet as soon as a Deployment with the same name appears
The old ReplicaSet is ignored permanently and keeps its Pods, while the new Deployment runs 3 separate Pods

bank.prompt: A ReplicaSet is running 3 Pods. For testing, you create a Pod by hand with exactly the same labels as those Pods, including the pod-template-hash label, and with no ownerReferences. Predict what happens and explain why.
bank.reference: The ReplicaSet controller sees an ownerless Pod that matches its selector and adopts it by adding an ownerReference that marks the ReplicaSet as its controller. The ReplicaSet now counts 4 Pods against a desired 3, so it deletes one of them. That could be your hand-made Pod or one of the originals.

bank.prompt: One Pod of a 3-replica Deployment has its container running, but its readiness probe keeps failing. What do you expect to see reported back up the chain?
bank.reference: The kubelet records a failed readiness probe as Ready false in the Pod's status. The ReplicaSet and Deployment controllers aggregate that into their ready replica counts, so readiness is reported up the chain without anything being restarted. The tempting confusion is with liveness probes: only a failing liveness probe makes the kubelet restart the container.
options: The Pod shows Running but not ready, and the Deployment and ReplicaSet report only 2 ready replicas
The kubelet restarts the container on each readiness failure, and the Pod's restart count keeps rising
The Deployment counts the Pod as ready because it is Running, so it still reports 3 of 3 ready
The ReplicaSet controller deletes the unready Pod and creates a replacement until one passes its probe

bank.concept: reading the chain with kubectl get and events
bank.prompt: The diagram shows the events from kubectl describe pod for a Pod that never becomes ready. Based on these events, which steps of the path from apply to a running container succeeded, which one failed, and where would you focus your investigation?
bank.reference: The Scheduled event from the scheduler shows the Pod was created and bound to a node. So the controllers, the API server and scheduling all worked. The kubelet events show it then failed to pull the image and is backing off. Focus on the image reference, the registry, or the pull credentials, not on scheduling or the controllers.

bank.concept: reading the chain with kubectl get and events
bank.prompt: A Pod named api-6f9c7b8d4-qz2lm is crash looping. Its namespace has several Deployments whose selectors all include app=api. What is the most reliable way to find which Deployment manages this Pod?
bank.reference: ownerReferences are the authoritative links, pointing from Pod to ReplicaSet and from ReplicaSet to Deployment. Here several selectors overlap, so matching by labels is ambiguous. Name prefixes are only a naming convention. The wide output of kubectl get deployments shows images and selectors, not Pod names.
options: Follow the Pod's ownerReferences to its ReplicaSet, then follow that ReplicaSet's ownerReferences to its Deployment
List the Deployments and pick the one whose label selector matches the labels set on this Pod
Strip the random suffixes from the Pod name and look up the Deployment whose name equals the remaining prefix
Run kubectl get deployments -o wide, which lists the names of the Pods that each Deployment manages

modules.title: When components fail
modules.objective: Predict the visible symptoms when the API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager or a kubelet is unavailable or slow.
concepts: running workloads survive control plane outages
node not ready and pod eviction timing
leader election in high availability control planes

bank.concept: running workloads survive control plane outages
bank.prompt: The only API server in a small cluster crashes and stays down for 20 minutes. What happens to the nginx pods that were already running on the worker nodes during that time?
bank.reference: Containers run under the kubelet and container runtime on each node, and the kubelet applies the restart policy locally without needing the API server. The tempting mistake is assuming every action needs the control plane; only changes that require writing to or reading new state from the API are blocked.
options: They keep running and serving traffic, and the kubelet still restarts containers that crash
They keep running, but crashed containers are not restarted until the API server returns
The kubelet stops them after it fails to reach the API server for several minutes
They are marked failed and rescheduled onto other nodes once the API server returns

bank.prompt: All kube-scheduler instances are stopped, but the API server and controller manager are healthy. You create a Deployment with 3 replicas. What does kubectl get pods show a minute later?
bank.reference: The controller manager creates the ReplicaSet and the pod objects, but only the scheduler sets a node on each pod, so they stay Pending with no nodeName. Seeing no pods at all would point to the controller manager being down, not the scheduler.
options: Three pods in Pending with no node assigned
No pods at all, only the Deployment and ReplicaSet objects
Three pods stuck in ContainerCreating on arbitrary nodes
Nothing, because the API server rejects the Deployment without a scheduler

bank.prompt: Every kube-controller-manager instance is down, while the API server, scheduler and kubelets are fine. You delete one of the three pods of the Deployment web. Predict how many web pods exist over the next ten minutes and explain why.
bank.reference: Only two pods remain and no replacement appears. The API server accepts the delete and the kubelet stops the containers, but creating a replacement is the job of the ReplicaSet controller, which runs inside the controller manager, so nothing reconciles the count back to three until it returns.

bank.concept: node not ready and pod eviction timing
bank.prompt: The timeline in the diagram shows a worker node losing its network at t = 0 and its pods later being evicted. Which setting mainly controls the length of interval B?
bank.reference: Once the node lifecycle controller marks the node and adds a NoExecute taint, pods stay until their toleration for that taint expires, which is 300 seconds by default via tolerations added at admission. The node monitor grace period is the tempting answer, but it governs interval A, the time before the node is marked Unknown and tainted.
options: The tolerationSeconds on the pods for the not-ready and unreachable taints
The node monitor grace period configured on the controller manager
The terminationGracePeriodSeconds field in each pod spec
The kubelet's hard eviction thresholds for memory and disk

bank.concept: node not ready and pod eviction timing
bank.prompt: A worker node loses power. About six minutes later kubectl get pods shows a new replica of your Deployment Running on another node, while the old pod on the dead node shows Terminating and never goes away. Explain why the old pod is stuck and why the replacement was still created.
bank.reference: Eviction only sets a deletion timestamp; the pod object is removed once the kubelet confirms the containers stopped, and the kubelet on the dead node cannot report back, so it stays Terminating. The ReplicaSet controller does not count pods that are being deleted, so it created a replacement that the scheduler placed on a healthy node.

bank.concept: leader election in high availability control planes
bank.prompt: A cluster has three control plane nodes, each running kube-scheduler with leader election enabled. At any given moment, how many scheduler instances are actively assigning pods to nodes?
bank.reference: The scheduler and controller manager are active-passive: instances compete for a Lease object and only the holder does work, while the others keep trying to acquire it. The tempting idea of work sharing or majority voting confuses these components with the API servers, which are all active, and with etcd, which uses quorum.
options: One, holding the lease, while the other two wait on standby
Three, each scheduling pods for its own share of the nodes
Three, with conflicting bindings resolved by the API server
Two, because a majority must agree on each placement

bank.concept: leader election in high availability control planes
bank.prompt: In the HA control plane shown, cp-1 holds the leases for both the scheduler and the controller manager, and then it loses power. Describe what users of the cluster notice, and roughly how long it lasts.
bank.reference: Running workloads are unaffected and the API stays available through cp-2 and cp-3 behind the load balancer, with etcd keeping quorum at two of three members. Scheduling and controller actions such as replacing pods pause briefly until cp-1's leases expire, typically seconds (on the order of the lease duration), after which standby instances acquire the leases and resume work.

bank.figure_alt: A load balancer in front of three control plane nodes, each running an API server, an etcd member, a scheduler and a controller manager, with cp-1 labelled as the lease holder.

bank.concept: running workloads survive control plane outages
bank.prompt: All etcd members in your cluster are down, while the API server processes are still running. Which of these continues to work normally during the outage?
bank.reference: Data-plane traffic flows through containers and the forwarding rules kube-proxy has already programmed, none of which need etcd. The API server does not queue writes; without etcd, writes such as scaling or binding a scheduled pod simply fail, so nothing new can be created or placed.
options: Existing pods keep serving traffic through Service rules already programmed on nodes
kubectl scale requests are accepted and queued until etcd recovers
New pods are still scheduled because the scheduler works from its own cache
Kubelets keep containers running only if they can confirm their state in etcd

bank.prompt: New pods in every namespace sit in Pending. kubectl describe pod shows no events at all, not even a FailedScheduling message. Existing pods are fine. What is the most likely cause?
bank.reference: When the scheduler runs but cannot place a pod, it records a FailedScheduling event explaining why, so silence suggests nothing is attempting to schedule. Image pull failures happen after a node is assigned, and a controller manager outage would mean pod objects were never created rather than created and Pending.
options: The scheduler is not running, or no instance holds the leader lease
No node has enough free CPU or memory for the pods' requests
The container images cannot be pulled from the registry
The controller manager is down, so the pods were never processed

bank.prompt: During a scheduler outage you urgently need one diagnostic pod running on a specific healthy node. Which pod would actually start without the scheduler?
bank.reference: Setting nodeName directly is what the scheduler would otherwise do, so the kubelet on that node sees the pod and starts it. A nodeSelector, priority class or small requests are only inputs to the scheduler's decision; without a running scheduler those pods still wait in Pending.
options: A pod whose spec sets nodeName to that node
A pod with a nodeSelector that matches only that node
A pod with a high priority class that allows preemption
A single-replica Deployment with no resource requests

bank.prompt: The controller manager has crashed, but the API server and scheduler are healthy. You run kubectl scale on Deployment web from 3 to 5 replicas. What do you observe?
bank.reference: The API server validates and stores the new desired state, but turning replicas into pod objects is done by the Deployment and ReplicaSet controllers in the controller manager, so actual state lags desired state. New Pending pods would be the symptom of a scheduler outage, not a controller manager one.
options: The command succeeds and the spec shows 5, but the pod count stays at 3
The command fails because the controller manager must validate scaling
Two new pods appear immediately but stay Pending without a node
The kubelets notice the new replica count and start two pods locally

bank.prompt: With the controller manager down for an hour, compare what you see when one pod's container keeps crashing versus when a whole worker node dies. Explain which failure still gets handled and which does not.
bank.reference: The crashing container is still restarted by its kubelet, so you see restarts and CrashLoopBackOff as usual. The dead node is not handled: the node lifecycle controller in the controller manager never marks it not ready or taints it, so its pods keep showing Running and no replacements are created elsewhere.

bank.concept: node not ready and pod eviction timing
bank.prompt: A latency-sensitive service loses capacity for over five minutes whenever a node dies, because its pods are only replaced after the default eviction delay. What change shortens that delay for this service without affecting other workloads?
bank.reference: Explicit tolerations with a short tolerationSeconds replace the default 300 second ones, so these pods are evicted and replaced sooner, at the cost of needless rescheduling during brief network blips. Grace periods and liveness probes are enforced by the kubelet, which on a dead node is not running, and kubelet eviction thresholds handle resource pressure rather than node loss.
options: Add tolerations for the not-ready and unreachable taints with a short tolerationSeconds
Lower terminationGracePeriodSeconds so evicted pods shut down faster
Lower the kubelet's hard eviction thresholds on every node
Add a liveness probe with a shorter period and failure threshold

bank.concept: node not ready and pod eviction timing
bank.prompt: A node becomes unreachable. After eviction, a Deployment pod from that node is replaced elsewhere, but StatefulSet pod db-0 just shows Terminating and no new db-0 appears anywhere. Why does the StatefulSet behave differently?
bank.reference: StatefulSets guarantee at most one pod per identity, so the controller waits until the old db-0 is gone, which cannot happen while the kubelet is unreachable unless an operator force deletes it or the node is removed. The pod is already Terminating, so eviction timing is not the issue, and no replacement pod even exists yet for the scheduler to hold back.
options: The StatefulSet will not create a new db-0 until the old pod object is actually removed
The scheduler will not place db-0 while its volume is still attached to the old node
The PodDisruptionBudget for the database blocks creating a replacement pod
StatefulSet pods get a much longer default toleration than Deployment pods

bank.concept: leader election in high availability control planes
bank.prompt: Your etcd cluster has 3 members, and a colleague proposes adding a fourth for more resilience. Raft needs a quorum of \( q = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor + 1 \) members to elect a leader and accept writes. What is the effect of the change?
bank.reference: With 4 members the quorum is 3, so losing 2 leaves no majority and writes stop, the same 1-failure tolerance as 3 members but with one more machine that can fail. Half is not a majority, which is why the tempting 2-failure answer is wrong; even-sized clusters can still elect a leader, they just add no fault tolerance.
options: No gain: 4 members still tolerate only 1 failure, so go to 5 to tolerate 2
It tolerates 2 failures, since 2 of 4 members is still half of the cluster
It tolerates 3 failures, since any single surviving member can serve writes
No gain, and it tolerates 0 failures because even sizes cannot elect a leader
